title: Building a Chat App
subtitle: From 2 friends to 2 million users
description: Follow the journey of a simple chat app as it grows from a weekend project to a platform serving millions. Along the way, you'll discover why systems break at scale — and the elegant solutions engineers have invented to fix them.

stages.title: Just You and a Friend

narrative.setup: You just built a chat app over the weekend. It's nothing fancy — a text box, a send button, and messages that appear on screen. You and your friend are the only users. Everything works perfectly.

blocks.content:
Congratulations — you shipped something! Your chat app is live. You type a message, hit send, and your friend sees it almost instantly. Life is good.

But let's peek under the hood. Even this simple app has a structure that every application on the internet shares. It's called the [[glossary:client-server|client-server model]].

Think of your app like a restaurant. **The client** (your browser) is the customer placing an order. **The server** is the kitchen receiving the order and sending back food. The customer never walks into the kitchen — they communicate through a waiter (the internet).

Right now, your setup is about as simple as it gets:

1. **[[node:client-1|Your browser]]** (the client) sends a message to [[node:server|the server]]
2. [[node:server|The server]] receives it and sends it to [[node:client-2|your friend's browser]]
3. Your friend's browser displays the message

That's it. One client, one server, two happy users.

blocks.caption: Your app right now — simple as it gets

blocks.content: Every app you've ever used — Instagram, Slack, Uber — started with this same basic pattern: a client talks to a server. The difference is what happens when millions of clients show up at once.

There's one thing to notice right now: your [[node:server|server]] is keeping all the messages **in memory**. That means they live in the server's temporary workspace — like writing notes on a whiteboard. Fast and easy, but...

blocks.question: What happens to your chat messages if the server restarts?

options.explanation: Exactly right. Data stored in memory is temporary — it vanishes when the server stops. It's like erasing a whiteboard. This will become a real problem very soon...
Not yet! Right now the messages only exist in the server's memory (RAM). Memory is wiped clean every time the server restarts. We'll need something more permanent.

options.text: They're stored in the user's browser
options.explanation: The browser only shows messages — it doesn't store the full history. Once you refresh, the browser asks the server for messages again. And if the server forgot them... they're gone.

suggestedQuestions: What exactly is a server? Is it a physical computer somewhere?
Why can't both people just connect directly without a server?
What does 'in memory' mean in simple terms?

stages.title: 100 Friends Join

narrative.setup: You shared your app on social media. A hundred friends and friends-of-friends signed up overnight. People are creating group chats, sharing memes, making plans.
narrative.problem: Then someone reports a bug: 'I sent a message last night but it's gone this morning.' You check — the server restarted overnight (servers do that sometimes), and every single message was lost. Your users are not happy.
narrative.resolution: You need a database — a permanent home for your data that survives server restarts.

blocks.content:
Things were going great — until they weren't.

Your [[node:server|server]] restarted overnight (a routine update from your hosting provider), and **every message disappeared**. Poof. Gone. A hundred users woke up to empty chat rooms.

Storing data in memory is like writing notes on a whiteboard in your office. Great for quick access, but if someone erases the board (or you switch offices), everything is lost. What you need is a **filing cabinet** — somewhere permanent to store things.

That filing cabinet is called a [[glossary:database|database]]. A database stores your data on disk (not just in memory), so it survives restarts, crashes, and updates.

Here's how your app works now:

1. User sends a message → server receives it
2. [[node:server|Server]] **writes the message to the [[node:database|database]]** (permanent storage)
3. Server sends the message to other users in the chat
4. When someone opens the app, the server **reads their messages from the database**

No more disappearing messages.

blocks.caption: Adding a database — your messages now survive restarts

blocks.content:
The most popular type of database for structured data like chat messages is a [[glossary:relational-database|relational database]] (like PostgreSQL or MySQL). It stores data in tables — think spreadsheets with rows and columns.

Your messages table might look like:

| id | chat_room | sender | message | sent_at |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | general | alice | hey everyone! | 2024-01-15 9:00am |
| 2 | general | bob | 👋 hello! | 2024-01-15 9:01am |
| 3 | random | charlie | check this out | 2024-01-15 9:02am |

Notice how the database is a **separate system** from your server. This is a fundamental pattern in system design: **separate your compute (the server that runs your code) from your storage (the database that holds your data)**. This way, if your server crashes, your data is safe.

blocks.scenario: Your chat app is growing! But users in the 'general' chat room are complaining that loading the chat history takes 5+ seconds. The room has 50,000 messages. Every time someone opens the room, your server asks the database for ALL 50,000 messages.
blocks.question: What's the smartest first fix?

options.text: Only load the last 50 messages, then load more as the user scrolls up
options.explanation: This is called **pagination** — loading data in small chunks instead of all at once. It's the same pattern you see on Twitter/X (infinite scroll) or Google (page 1, 2, 3). It's almost always the right first move for large datasets.

options.text: Buy a faster, more powerful server
options.explanation: This is called **vertical scaling** — making your single machine beefier. It works up to a point, but it's expensive and has hard limits. A $10,000 server won't load 50K messages much faster if the real problem is that you're requesting too much data at once.

options.text: Delete old messages to keep the database small
options.explanation: Users generally don't love having their messages deleted! This might work for ephemeral content (like Snapchat), but for a chat app people want their history. There are much better solutions.

blocks.label: Want to go deeper? How does the database actually store data on disk?
blocks.content:
When you write a message to a database like PostgreSQL, here's what actually happens:

1. The message arrives at the database server
2. It's first written to a **write-ahead log** (WAL) — a sequential record that ensures no data is lost even if the power goes out mid-write
3. Then it's organized into the table's **data file** on disk, indexed so it can be found quickly later

This is why databases are reliable — they're designed to survive crashes at any point in the write process. Your data is safe even if someone trips over the power cord.

suggestedQuestions: What's the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
How does the database find a specific message so quickly?
Should I use PostgreSQL or MySQL for my app?

stages.title: The Group Chat Explodes

narrative.setup: Your app hit 1,000 users. People love it. Group chats are active all day. But users are starting to complain about something new: messages feel 'laggy.' They send a message and it takes a few seconds before others see it.
narrative.problem: You discover the issue: your app checks for new messages by asking the server 'any new messages?' every 3 seconds. With 1,000 users all doing this simultaneously, your server is drowning in 'are we there yet?' requests — most of which get the answer 'nope, nothing new.'
narrative.resolution: You need to switch from polling to WebSockets — a technology that lets the server push messages to clients instantly, without them having to ask.

blocks.content:
Your users are complaining: *"Why does it take so long for messages to appear?"*

Let's figure out why. Right now, your app uses a technique called [[glossary:polling|polling]] to check for new messages. Here's how it works:

Imagine you're waiting for a package. **Polling** is like walking to your front door every 30 seconds to check: *"Is it here yet? Is it here yet? Is it here yet?"* Most trips, there's nothing there. It's exhausting — for you and for the delivery person who has to keep answering the door.

Your app does the same thing:

1. Every 3 seconds, each client asks the server: *"Any new messages?"*
2. The server checks the database and responds (usually with *"Nope"*)
3. Multiply this by 1,000 users = **~333 requests per second** just for checking

Most of these requests are completely wasted — there's nothing new to report. But your server has to handle every single one. It's like having 1,000 kids in a car all asking *"Are we there yet?"* at the same time.

The fix is a technology called [[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]]. Instead of the client constantly asking for updates, a WebSocket creates a **persistent, two-way connection** between the client and [[node:server|server]].

WebSockets are like a **phone call** instead of texting. With texting (polling), you send a message and wait for a reply each time. With a phone call (WebSocket), you open a line and both sides can talk whenever they have something to say — no need to keep dialing.

With WebSockets:

1. When a user opens the app, their browser opens a WebSocket connection to the server (like picking up the phone)
2. The connection **stays open** as long as the user is on the app
3. When someone sends a message, [[node:server|the server]] **immediately pushes** it to every connected client in that chat room
4. No more asking. No more waiting. Messages appear **instantly**.

This is how every real-time app works — Slack, Discord, WhatsApp Web, Google Docs collaboration.

blocks.caption: WebSockets: persistent connections replace constant polling

blocks.scenario: You've switched to WebSockets and messages are now instant. But you notice something: when a user's internet connection drops for 30 seconds and reconnects, they're missing the messages that were sent during the disconnect.
blocks.question: How would you handle this?

options.text: When reconnecting, fetch missed messages from the database using a timestamp
options.explanation: This is the standard approach. When a client reconnects, it tells the server: *"Last message I saw was at 9:15:32 AM."* The server queries the database for everything after that time and sends it over. This combines the best of both worlds: real-time delivery via WebSockets, with the database as a reliable backup.

options.text: Just accept that some messages might be lost
options.explanation: For a chat app, losing messages is unacceptable — people are having real conversations! This might be okay for something like a live stock ticker where old data is irrelevant, but not for messaging.

options.text: Keep the old polling system as a backup alongside WebSockets
options.explanation: This adds complexity without much benefit. You'd have two systems doing similar jobs. The simpler approach is to use WebSockets for real-time delivery and the database for catching up on anything missed. You already have both — just use them together.

blocks.content: Notice a pattern here: **the database isn't just for saving data — it's your safety net**. WebSockets handle the fast, real-time delivery. The database handles reliability and history. This pattern of combining a fast-but-fragile system with a slow-but-reliable one shows up everywhere in system design.

blocks.label: Curious? How does a WebSocket connection actually work?
blocks.content:
A WebSocket connection starts as a regular HTTP request (the same kind your browser makes to load any webpage). But it includes a special header that says: *"Hey, I'd like to upgrade this to a WebSocket connection."*

If the server agrees, the connection is "upgraded" — instead of the usual request-response cycle (ask → answer → hang up), the connection stays open. Both sides can now send data at any time.

Technically:
1. Client sends: `GET /chat HTTP/1.1` with `Upgrade: websocket` header
2. Server responds: `101 Switching Protocols`
3. Now both sides can send frames (small packets of data) whenever they want

The connection stays open until one side explicitly closes it, or the network drops.

suggestedQuestions: How many WebSocket connections can one server handle?
Is there a middle ground between polling and WebSockets?
How do apps like Discord handle millions of concurrent connections?
